sm: The episode opens with Ayn Rand arriving in America in 1926 as a young Russian immigrant, struck by the freedom and optimism of the roaring twenties. The host, Maggie, argues the twenties boom was real, driven by the pro-capitalist policies of President Calvin Coolidge and Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon. Top tax rates fell from 73 percent to 25 percent, federal spending was trimmed, debt fell by a quarter, and wages rose while working hours dropped. She says the Fed, convinced the market was a bubble, raised interest rates, which spooked investors and led to the October 1929 crash and about nine thousand bank failures. Unemployment hit 25 percent, and she blames Hoover's Smoot-Hawley tariff, which cut trade by two thirds, and his 1932 tax increase to 63 percent.

Maggie says Franklin Roosevelt won in 1932 promising sound money and balanced budgets, but broke nearly every promise except ending Prohibition. She says he blamed capitalism, left the gold standard, seized private gold, and pushed the New Deal, including the National Industrial Recovery Act and the Agricultural Adjustment Act, which she calls heavy-handed control of business. Unemployment was still around 14 percent before World War Two, and she argues the war did not end the Depression. She credits the postwar recovery to a 68 percent cut in federal spending, a return to a gold-linked dollar, and a 1946 free trade agreement. She links the era to Rand, Leonard Read and Ronald Reagan, and says her view remains a minority one.
